title: merz macron yuan focus gets china backwards 2026 08 31
author: Hudson Lockett
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 31 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Europe’s largest economies are finally on the same page about China. Unfortunately, it’s the wrong one. French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz ​plan to release a joint roadmap
, opens new tab
 next month for bringing down their largest trading partner’s surplus, which per China customs
, opens new tab
 totalled ‌a whopping $687 billion between January and July. They are focused on getting the yuan to appreciate, which is meant to boost Chinese consumption and imports.
This gets things exactly backwards. Demand must first rise to spur imports and the exchange rate higher, which requires convincing Beijing to fully commit to its so-far ​halfhearted drive to revive household spending.
Merz isn’t necessarily wrong when he argues
, opens new tab
 the yuan is undervalued by some 25%. But ​China’s cost advantage goes far beyond its currency. The People's Republic is also fearful of repeating the 1985 ⁠Plaza Accord, in which several nations agreed to appreciate their currencies against the U.S. dollar, as top cadres believe this played a ​key role in Japan's economic excruciation during the 1990s. If European negotiators want more effective leverage, they can focus on a pain ​point closer to home: unemployment.
The Communist party despises the mere suggestion of widespread joblessness, enough that the headline unemployment rate rarely deviates from 5%. This helps justify President Xi Jinping’s opposition
, opens new tab
 to expanding China’s welfare state, but less sensitive stats suggest it’s growing anyways. Last year, recipients of jobless benefits rose to ​5.6 million, a new high for this century. Meanwhile researchers at the Capital University of Economics and Business forecast flexible employment, a yardstick ​for precarious low-wage work and proxy for underemployment, to reach 320 million people this year. That's double pre-pandemic levels
, opens new tab
.
Those woes' origin lies in Xi’s 2020 ‌campaign targeting ⁠highly indebted developers. Deleveraging attempts torpedoed real estate as a driver of Chinese economic growth and, as a result, torched household wealth. Families responded by saving more, hobbling domestic demand. Inflation cratered, causing officials to cut interest rates, which weakened the yuan.
To be sure, policymakers have been somewhat tolerant of this outcome because it has benefited exporters in strategic sectors like electric vehicles. But this doesn't mean, as ​Brussels insiders sometimes assume, that depressed ​demand is the end-goal. Exporters ⁠alone aren't a large enough chunk of the economy to ensure robust employment, hence Beijing's roll-out of piecemeal plans to revive consumer spending.
If Europe wants a stronger yuan and balanced trade, then, its ​greatest hope lies in China taking more forceful action, such as finally putting a floor under ​falling property prices. ⁠This would leave a sour taste in Xi’s mouth but it's better than rising unemployment and punitive EU countermeasures. If European negotiators want to add rhetorical oomph to their case, they can describe it in the party's own parlance
, opens new tab
: "win-win cooperation”.
